characters: Adu: an eight-year-old Ghanaian boy with short neat hair in a red-and-khaki school sports kit, holding a classic black-and-white ball.
Dery: his eight-year-old Ghanaian girl classmate with neat braids in a matching red-and-blue school sports shirt and skirt.
Their teacher: an encouraging Ghanaian female teacher in a clean blue collared sports polo shirt and dark trousers.

narrationPlan.voice: A cheerful boy’s voice for Adu; an inquisitive girl’s voice for Dery
narrationPlan.pace: Quick and bouncy during play, then slower (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A playground tune with a bouncing beat (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Ball games are a favourite at break time in Ghanaian schools. The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on parts of the body that work together (B2.3.1.1.1, B3.3.1.1.1).
The story keeps to simple ideas: senses tell the brain, the brain sends messages, muscles and bones move the body.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the simple description of how senses, brain, muscles and bones work together against NaCCA B2.3.1.1.1 and B3.3.1.1.1.
Check the statement that the heart pumps blood and breath brings air.

teacherGuide.overview: Catching a ball shows how eyes, brain, legs, hands, heart and lungs work together. Children learn simple body parts and keeping the body healthy. Based on NaCCA Science standards on body systems.
learningGoals: Name body parts used in catching a ball.
Name two ways to keep the body strong.
beforeReading: Ask: what body parts do we use to catch a ball?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 and trace the message from eyes to brain to hands.
afterReading: Play catch with a soft ball and name each body part used.
discussion: What would happen if the eyes could not see?
How can we look after our bodies?
reflection: Which part of your body team do you thank today?

support: Use a body picture and arrows.
stretch: Compare the body to a team on a football pitch.

culturalNotes: Ball games are a favourite at break time in Ghanaian schools. The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on parts of the body that work together (B2.3.1.1.1, B3.3.1.1.1).
The story keeps to simple ideas: senses tell the brain, the brain sends messages, muscles and bones move the body.
localiseThis: Use the games your children play: ball, skipping, running.
Remind children that people with different abilities can all join in games.
